title: Dominion theology: theonomy, Kingdom Now and the Seven Mountains
question: Are Christians called to bring the institutions of society, including civil government and law, under the explicit rule of Christ before he returns, and if so, by what standard and by what means?
intro:
"Dominion theology" is an umbrella term, used mostly by critics, for views holding that Christians are commissioned to extend Christ's rule over every sphere of society. The name comes from Genesis 1:28, where humanity is told to exercise dominion over the earth, a text often called the cultural mandate.

The label covers two streams that differ sharply. The first is Christian Reconstruction, or theonomy. It comes out of conservative Presbyterianism and is associated with R. J. Rushdoony, Greg Bahnsen and Gary North. It holds that Old Testament law, civil penalties included, remains the standard for modern states, and it expects the gospel to triumph gradually in history (postmillennialism). The second is a charismatic stream. It runs from Earl Paulk's "Kingdom Now" teaching in the 1980s to the "Seven Mountains" mandate popularised by Lance Wallnau and Johnny Enlow, and it speaks of believers gaining influence at the top of seven spheres of culture under the guidance of present-day apostles and prophets.

Critics range widely: Reformed theologians such as Meredith Kline and the Westminster Seminary faculty, dispensationalists, two-kingdoms advocates, Anabaptists, and journalists and scholars who study Christian nationalism. Many people placed under the label reject the word "dominionism" as a caricature. This entry sets out each stream in its own terms, then the critics' case, with historical evidence on both sides.

positions.name: Christian Reconstruction (theonomy)
positions.summary:
Christian Reconstruction teaches that God's revealed law, including the civil statutes and penal sanctions of the Old Testament, remains binding in every area of life unless the New Testament itself revokes or modifies it. That includes civil government. The ceremonial law is fulfilled in Christ, but the judicial law still expresses God's unchanging justice and should guide modern magistrates by its "general equity."

The system rests on three supports. The first is Cornelius Van Til's presuppositional apologetics: no law-system is religiously neutral, so every society is governed by some god's law. The second is postmillennial eschatology: the gospel will progressively triumph in history. The third is a decentralist political vision: family, church and local community carry most of life, and the state is limited. Leading Reconstructionists insisted that change must come by regeneration and persuasion over generations, not by revolution or coup.

figures.name: Rousas John Rushdoony
figures.profession: Presbyterian minister, writer, founder of the Chalcedon Foundation
figures.bio: Rushdoony was born in New York to Armenian parents who had fled the genocide in Ottoman Turkey. He served as a missionary on the Duck Valley reservation in Nevada and then as a pastor. In 1965 he founded the Chalcedon Foundation in California. His massive *Institutes of Biblical Law* (1973) works through the Ten Commandments as the framework for all law. He was an early advocate of Christian schooling and homeschooling and testified for homeschooling families in court.

works.title: The Messianic Character of American Education

figures.name: Greg L. Bahnsen
figures.profession: Philosopher, apologist, Orthodox Presbyterian minister
figures.bio: Bahnsen trained at Westminster Theological Seminary and earned a PhD in philosophy at the University of Southern California. His *Theonomy in Christian Ethics* (1977) gave the movement its most rigorous exegetical defence, arguing for the abiding validity of the law "in exhaustive detail." The controversy it caused contributed to his departure from Reformed Theological Seminary in Jackson. He was also a leading presuppositional debater, notably against the atheist Gordon Stein in 1985.

figures.name: Gary North
figures.profession: Economic historian, author, publisher
figures.bio: North held a PhD in history from the University of California, Riverside. He was Rushdoony's son-in-law until the two men fell out in the early 1980s. Through the Institute for Christian Economics in Tyler, Texas, he published a huge volume of material applying biblical law to economics, money and politics. He was the movement's most combative popularizer. In the late 1990s his warnings that the Y2K computer problem would cause social collapse drew wide criticism when the collapse did not come.

figures.bio: Gentry is a leading defender of postmillennialism and of preterist readings of prophecy. Both give theonomy its optimistic view of history. With Bahnsen he answered dispensationalist critics in *House Divided* (1989).

figures.profession: Writer, president of American Vision
figures.bio: DeMar brought Reconstructionist ideas to a popular evangelical audience through books, curricula and American Vision. He has stressed self-government under God and the bottom-up, non-coercive character of the program.

positions.context:
Reconstruction emerged in 1960s America, which was rapidly secularizing. The Supreme Court had removed state-sponsored prayer from public schools (1962-63), and many conservative Protestants saw public education and law cutting loose from any Christian basis. Rushdoony combined Van Til's claim that neutrality is impossible with the Puritan precedent of Mosaic-based law codes. He offered a full alternative to secular humanism.

The movement was always small, and it split early between Rushdoony's Chalcedon in California and North's group in Tyler, Texas. Its indirect influence was larger than its numbers. It shaped the legal defence of homeschooling, Christian school curricula and the vocabulary of the 1980s Religious Right, though most Religious Right leaders did not accept theonomy's penal code. A renewed online interest in theonomy and postmillennialism among younger Reformed Christians appeared in the 2010s and 2020s.
claims: Every sphere of life, including civil government, ought to be governed by God's revealed law. That is what 'theonomy' means: God's law as opposed to self-made law.
Old Testament commandments remain binding unless the New Testament revokes or modifies them. The burden of proof lies on discontinuity.
The ceremonial and sacrificial laws are fulfilled in Christ. The judicial laws, including their penal sanctions, express God's justice and still guide magistrates by their general equity.
No society is religiously neutral. Secular law simply enthrones a different ultimate authority.
The gospel will progressively triumph in history before Christ returns (postmillennialism).
Reconstruction comes from the bottom up, through regeneration, families, churches and voluntary adoption over generations, not through revolution or forced conversion.
Biblical law favours a sharply limited civil government, protection of private property, restitution in place of prisons, and honest money.

scriptures.reading: Jesus came not to abolish the law but to confirm it, and the least commandment remains. Theonomists read this as a presumption of continuity for the whole law.
Israel's statutes were meant to make the nations marvel at their righteousness. The civil law was therefore designed as a model for other peoples, not only for Israel.
The dominion mandate given to humanity is renewed in Christ, and redeemed people are to exercise it in every area of culture under God's law.
The magistrate is 'God's minister' who punishes evildoers. If he serves God, God must define what counts as evil and what punishment is just.
Paul says the law is good when used lawfully against the lawless and lists crimes that follow the Decalogue. The law still has a civil and restraining use.
Every transgression under the Mosaic order received a 'just recompence'. Bahnsen used this to argue that the New Testament itself calls the Mosaic penalties just.
Kings and judges of the earth are commanded to serve the Lord and kiss the Son, which implies that rulers owe accountability to Christ as rulers.
All authority belongs to Christ, and nations are to be discipled and taught to observe everything he commanded. The Great Commission is read as reaching whole cultures.
Faith does not make the law void. It establishes the law.

arguments.text: In Matthew 5:17-19 Jesus affirms that the law remains, down to its least stroke. So any commandment continues unless Scripture itself shows it has changed, as it does for sacrifices and food laws. Nothing in the New Testament explicitly repeals the civil penalties.
Deuteronomy presents Israel's laws as wisdom the nations should admire. A law meant to be exemplary cannot be purely local or arbitrary.

Neutrality is impossible. Every legal code rests on some view of the ultimate good. Christians must therefore choose between God's law and some human or idolatrous standard, and declining to choose simply hands public life to secular humanism.
God's character does not change. If he once called certain penalties just, they do not become unjust because the setting changes. Only a revealed change in God's will could alter them.

The Reformed tradition has precedent. John Cotton drafted a code for Massachusetts (1636) based on Mosaic judicial law, and the Massachusetts Body of Liberties (1641) cited Scripture for its capital laws. Puritan theologians debated how the 'general equity' of Moses applied, which shows the question was not invented in 1973.

Westminster Confession 19.4 says the judicial laws expired with Israel's state, but adds that they oblige no further 'than the general equity thereof may require'. Theonomists argue this reservation was meant to keep the substance of those laws in force.

Biblical law limits the state severely. It has no prisons in the modern sense, no standing tax of the modern scale and no central bureaucracy, so Reconstructionists argue that their system restrains tyranny rather than enlarging it.

critiques.from: Meredith G. Kline (Westminster Theological Journal, 1978)
critiques.text: Israel's theocracy was a unique, typological 'intrusion' of final judgment into history, bound to the holy land and covenant. Its penal sanctions foreshadow the last judgment. They are not a template for common-grace states, which God appoints for temporary order among believers and unbelievers alike.

critiques.from: Westminster Seminary faculty, *Theonomy: A Reformed Critique* (1990)
critiques.text: Theonomy misreads its own confessional tradition. 'General equity' in WCF 19.4 refers to the underlying moral principles, not the specific penalties. In Matthew 5:17 'fulfil' is christological and eschatological, not a simple continuation of the Mosaic code, and the New Testament nowhere asks pagan rulers to adopt Mosaic law.

critiques.from: Dispensationalist critics (H. Wayne House and Thomas Ice, 1988)
critiques.text: Theonomy confuses Israel with the church and the present age with the millennium. The New Testament expects growing apostasy and persecution before Christ's return, not a gradual Christianization of the world.

critiques.from: Civil libertarians, journalists and many evangelical ethicists
critiques.text: Applying Mosaic penalties today would mean the death penalty for blasphemy, idolatry, adultery, homosexual acts or incorrigible children, as several Reconstructionist writers allowed. That would destroy religious liberty and the equal citizenship of non-Christians.

critiques.from: Two-kingdoms theologians (e.g. David VanDrunen)
critiques.text: The church's mission is word, sacrament and discipleship. The civil kingdom is governed by natural law under common grace, and the church as an institution has no mandate to transform it into a Christian commonwealth.

responses.text: Bahnsen replied that Kline's 'intrusion ethic' leaves magistrates with no revealed standard of justice at all, and that the New Testament treats the Mosaic penalties as just and as instruction for magistrates.

In *No Other Standard* (1991) Bahnsen argued that seventeenth-century Reformed writers, including many divines who taught 'general equity', did apply Mosaic penalties for crimes such as blasphemy and adultery. On that reading the theonomic interpretation is closer to the Westminster divines than the modern critics are.

Gentry and Bahnsen's *House Divided* (1989) argued that postmillennial hope rests on Christ's present enthronement and on parables of steady kingdom growth. They held that the apostasy passages refer mainly to the first-century crisis before AD 70.

Reconstructionists answer that biblical law demands two or three witnesses and strict due process, and treats many penalties as maximums. It never authorizes forced conversion. They add that it could only be adopted where a population had already been converted and consented, so they reject any picture of a theonomic regime imposed on an unwilling people.

Theonomists answer that natural law, read by fallen minds, gives no stable content without Scripture. On this view two-kingdoms theology effectively concedes public law to secularism and denies that Christ's lordship extends to rulers.

strawMen.strawMan: Theonomists want to seize power and impose Old Testament law by force.
strawMen.correction: Rushdoony, Bahnsen, North and DeMar all taught that biblical law could only rightly come through widespread conversion and consent over a long time. They rejected revolution, and most of their energy went into education, family and church.

strawMen.strawMan: Theonomy means keeping all the Old Testament law, including sacrifices, food laws and Sabbath-year rules.
strawMen.correction: Theonomists hold that the ceremonial and sacrificial laws are fulfilled in Christ. Their dispute with other Reformed Christians concerns the judicial laws and their penalties.

strawMen.strawMan: The Religious Right as a whole is Reconstructionist.
strawMen.correction: Reconstruction has always been a small movement, and most evangelical political leaders rejected its penal code. Its influence was real but mostly indirect, through homeschooling, presuppositional apologetics and talk of 'Christian worldview'.

positive: Supplied legal and intellectual support to the homeschooling movement in the United States.
Forced Reformed theologians to think carefully about the relation of the Mosaic law to modern ethics and the state.
Encouraged Christians to apply their faith to economics, education and law instead of treating faith as private.
Produced serious exegetical work on the law and on postmillennial eschatology.
negative: Its willingness to extend capital penalties to religious and sexual offences alarmed other Christians and non-Christians alike.
It became shorthand in public debate for Christian theocracy, at times tarring evangelicals who held no such views.
Internal feuds and some sensational predictions, such as Y2K collapse warnings, damaged its credibility.
Critics see a line from its rhetoric to present-day Christian nationalism, though the connection is debated.

adherents: Chalcedon Foundation and American Vision
Small networks within conservative Presbyterian and Reformed denominations
Parts of the Christian homeschooling and classical Christian education movements
A revived online theonomy and postmillennial scene among younger Reformed Christians since the 2010s

positions.name: Kingdom Now and the Seven Mountains mandate
positions.summary:
The charismatic stream of dominion thought holds that the kingdom of God is present and advancing, and that the church is God's agent for showing his rule in every part of society before Christ returns. In the 1980s Earl Paulk's "Kingdom Now" teaching argued that a mature church must first establish kingdom realities on earth.

From the 2000s the "Seven Mountains" mandate gave this vision a practical map. Culture is shaped from the top of seven spheres, or "mountains": religion, family, education, government, media, arts and entertainment, and business. Believers are urged to gain godly influence at the top of each one. Present-day apostles and prophets often give the strategy.

Most proponents describe the goal as influence through excellence and service, being salt and light. They do not seek theocracy. They usually have no interest in the Mosaic civil code, and their eschatology tends to be eclectic or 'victorious' rather than formally postmillennial.

figures.name: Earl Paulk
figures.profession: Pentecostal pastor, bishop of Chapel Hill Harvester Church (later Cathedral at Chapel Hill), Decatur, Georgia
figures.bio: Paulk came out of the Church of God (Cleveland, Tennessee) and built a large, racially integrated congregation near Atlanta. In the 1980s he taught that the church must demonstrate and establish the kingdom of God on earth, and that Christ's return waits on a mature, unified church. This 'Kingdom Now' teaching drew heavy criticism from other charismatics and evangelicals. Allegations of sexual misconduct later severely damaged his ministry.

figures.name: Loren Cunningham
figures.profession: Founder of Youth With A Mission (YWAM)
figures.bio: Cunningham founded YWAM in 1960. In his retelling, in 1975 he received a list of seven spheres, or 'mind-molders', of society that Christians should reach. When he met Campus Crusade founder Bill Bright soon afterwards, Bright had reportedly received a nearly identical list, and Francis Schaeffer is sometimes said to have spoken of something similar. Cunningham presented this as a missions and discipleship framework, not a political program. The account rests mainly on his own later testimony.

figures.name: C. Peter Wagner
figures.profession: Missiologist, Fuller Theological Seminary professor, convener of apostolic networks
figures.bio: Wagner had been a missionary in Bolivia and became a church-growth scholar. He named and organised the New Apostolic Reformation. Late in life he openly embraced 'dominion' language, arguing that the church is called to take dominion over society and that apostles in the workplace are key to transforming nations.

works.author: C. Peter Wagner
works.title: Dominion! How Kingdom Action Can Change the World

figures.name: Lance Wallnau
figures.profession: Charismatic speaker, business consultant
figures.bio: From the 2000s Wallnau was the best-known popularizer of 'Seven Mountain' language. He spoke of believers taking the high places of culture. In the 2016 election season he gained national attention by presenting Donald Trump as a providential 'Cyrus' figure. Critics and admirers alike treat him as the movement's leading public voice.

figures.name: Johnny Enlow
figures.profession: Charismatic pastor and author
figures.bio: Enlow's books gave the Seven Mountains idea a prophetic and allegorical treatment. Each mountain is said to be held by a particular demonic stronghold that believers must displace through prayer and godly influence.

positions.context:
Kingdom Now grew out of mid-century charismatic currents. These include the 1948 Latter Rain revival in Saskatchewan, with its expectation of restored apostles and prophets and a mature 'manifest' church, and the 1970s charismatic renewal. In the 1980s it sat beside, but separate from, Reconstruction. Critics often grouped the two together, while Reconstructionists such as Gary North kept their distance from charismatic theology even as some charismatic leaders borrowed Reconstructionist ideas.

The Seven Mountains framework spread in the 2000s through apostolic networks, business conferences and books. After 2016 it became tied in public perception to charismatic support for Donald Trump. Its global reach is significant in Latin America and Africa, where it often appears as encouragement for Christians to enter business and public service.
claims: The kingdom of God is a present reality advancing on earth, and the church is God's primary agent for showing his rule.
The cultural mandate of Genesis 1:28 is restored in Christ, so believers are called to steward and shape every part of society.
Culture is shaped disproportionately by those at the top of seven spheres, so transformation requires godly leaders there.
God has restored apostles and prophets who give strategic direction for transforming cities and nations.
Transforming a sphere involves spiritual warfare against demonic strongholds as well as practical excellence.
The aim is influence through service, integrity and excellence, being salt and light, not coercive rule or theocracy.
Christ's return is linked to the maturing of the church and the advance of the kingdom; how strongly this is held varies among proponents.

scriptures.reading: Humanity was created to exercise stewarding dominion over creation. Redemption restores this vocation to believers in every field of work.
The prayer that God's will be done on earth as in heaven is taken as a mandate to bring heaven's order into earthly institutions now.
Salt and light work by being present in and influencing the surrounding culture, not withdrawing from it.
The stone cut without hands grows into a great mountain that fills the whole earth. Enlow and others read this as the kingdom displacing the mountains of culture.
The mountain of the Lord's house is established above all other mountains. Proponents read this as the kingdom rising above every sphere of culture.
Of the increase of his government there will be no end. The kingdom's growth is continuous and expanding.
The kingdoms of this world become the kingdoms of the Lord and of his Christ, a goal the church works toward.
Creation waits for the revealing of the sons of God. In Latter Rain and Kingdom Now teaching this pointed to a mature church manifesting God's rule before the end.

arguments.text: Jesus taught his disciples to pray for God's will on earth as in heaven. A church that expects nothing to change on earth before the second coming has, on this view, stopped praying the prayer in earnest.
Daniel's stone becomes a mountain filling the earth, and Isaiah's kingdom grows without end. Scripture pictures the kingdom spreading through history, not only arriving at its end.

When Christians withdraw from media, education, the arts and government, others shape those spheres and Christians then complain about the results. Discipleship must therefore include preparing believers to lead in every vocation.

Christian influence has transformed societies before. Examples include Wilberforce and the Clapham Sect against the slave trade, and Abraham Kuyper's claim that Christ claims 'every square inch' of creation. Proponents see the Seven Mountains as a contemporary application of this tradition.
Cunningham and Bright are said to have received the same list of seven spheres independently in 1975. Proponents treat this as providential confirmation of the framework.
The seven-sphere scheme is a practical vocational map. It helps ordinary believers see business, art or teaching as ministry rather than secular work.

critiques.from: Theological critics (Bruce Barron; Holly Pivec and R. Douglas Geivett)
critiques.text: The teaching blurs the church's mission with the pursuit of social and political power. It reads kingdom texts with an over-realized eschatology and depends on unaccountable apostolic and prophetic authority for its strategy.

critiques.from: Journalists and scholars of Christian nationalism (Katherine Stewart; Matthew D. Taylor)
critiques.text: In practice, Seven Mountains rhetoric fused with partisan politics. Prophetic endorsements of a candidate, election-fraud claims after 2020 and 'spiritual warfare' framing around 6 January 2021 show how 'taking the mountain of government' can slide into hostility toward pluralist democracy.

critiques.from: Classical Pentecostals and evangelical discernment writers (e.g. Dave Hunt)
critiques.text: Kingdom Now revives Latter Rain ideas, such as a 'manifested' church conquering the world before Christ returns, which the Assemblies of God rejected in 1949. It also replaces the hope of Christ's return with the church's own achievement.

critiques.from: Pastoral critics inside and outside the charismatic movement
critiques.text: Apostolic networks with strong leaders and little external oversight have repeatedly produced moral and financial scandals, as in Earl Paulk's ministry. Critics say a theology of leaders seizing 'tops of mountains' feeds this.

responses.text: Wagner and others answered that 'dominion' means stewardship and godly influence, not ecclesiastical rule over the state. They argued the church has always sought to see justice and mercy shape society, as the abolitionists did.

Proponents argue that Christians voting, organizing and running for office is ordinary democratic participation, not theocracy, and that 'Christian nationalism' is used too loosely. Many charismatic leaders, including some sympathetic to the framework, publicly condemned the violence of 6 January 2021.
Kingdom Now advocates said their emphasis on the church's maturity is close to historic Puritan and postmillennial optimism, and that it complements rather than replaces hope in Christ's return.

Defenders reply that scandals reflect individual sin, not the framework. They point out that the Seven Mountains model is explicitly about humility and serving from below as well as leading from above.

strawMen.strawMan: The Seven Mountains mandate is a plan to take over the government by force.
strawMen.correction: Its proponents speak of influence, excellence and spiritual warfare in prayer, not armed seizure of power. Critics' real concern is the fusion of this framework with partisan politics and prophetic claims, not a literal coup plan.

strawMen.strawMan: Seven Mountains teachers are theonomists who want the Mosaic law code.
strawMen.correction: Most are charismatics with no interest in the Mosaic civil code or Reformed postmillennialism. The two streams differ in theology, ecclesiology and method.

strawMen.strawMan: Every charismatic who talks about 'the kingdom now' holds Kingdom Now theology.
strawMen.correction: Many charismatics, such as the Vineyard tradition shaped by George Ladd, teach that the kingdom is 'already and not yet' without any program for cultural dominion.

positive: Encouraged believers to see work in business, media, education and the arts as a calling.
Inspired social, educational and entrepreneurial projects, especially in the Global South.
Challenged a privatized faith that ignored public life.
negative: Became closely tied to partisan politics and failed election prophecies, damaging the credibility of the prophetic movement.
Encouraged triumphalism and a confusion of God's kingdom with national or political success.
Concentrated authority in self-appointed apostles with weak accountability.

adherents: Apostolic-prophetic networks associated with the New Apostolic Reformation
Some independent charismatic megachurches and prayer networks
Marketplace-ministry organisations in North and Latin America and Africa
Individual politicians and activists who use Seven Mountains language

positions.name: Critics: Reformed, two-kingdoms, dispensational and pluralist objections
positions.summary:
The critics share no single theology. Reformed scholars such as Meredith Kline and the Westminster faculty, two-kingdoms theologians, dispensationalists, Anabaptists, charismatic insiders and journalists all object to dominion programs, each for their own reasons.

Their common ground is that Christ's kingdom advances in this age mainly through word, Spirit and the church's witness, not by capturing civil power. On this view Israel's theocracy and its civil law belonged to a unique covenant that Christ fulfilled, the New Testament expects the church to live as pilgrims and often as sufferers until his return, and Christians serve their neighbours as citizens of pluralist societies while defending liberty of conscience for all. Most critics still affirm that Christians should take part in public life. Their dispute is about the standard, the means and the goal.

figures.name: Meredith G. Kline
figures.profession: Old Testament scholar, Westminster and Gordon-Conwell seminaries
figures.bio: Kline developed a covenantal reading of the Old Testament that treated Israel's theocracy as a typological 'intrusion' of the final kingdom. His 1978 review of Bahnsen was among the earliest and sharpest Reformed critiques of theonomy. His framework later shaped the two-kingdoms theology of Westminster Seminary California.

figures.name: W. Robert Godfrey
figures.profession: Church historian, president of Westminster Seminary California
figures.bio: With William S. Barker, Godfrey edited *Theonomy: A Reformed Critique* (1990). Its essays by Westminster faculty examined theonomy's exegesis, its reading of the confession and its practical implications.

works.title: Theonomy: A Reformed Critique

figures.name: David VanDrunen
figures.profession: Professor of systematic theology and ethics, Westminster Seminary California
figures.bio: VanDrunen is the leading contemporary advocate of Reformed two-kingdoms theology. He argues that civil life is governed by natural law under the Noahic covenant of common grace, while the church's distinct mission is the gospel.

figures.bio: Barron's 1992 study surveyed both Reconstructionists and charismatic dominion teachers. It took them seriously on their own terms, gave credit where due, and criticised their triumphalism and their handling of Scripture.

positions.context:
Criticism came in waves. In the late 1970s and 1980s Reformed scholars answered Bahnsen and Rushdoony, and dispensationalists answered both Reconstruction and Kingdom Now. In the 1990s sociologists such as Sara Diamond popularised 'dominionism' as a category for the Religious Right. Since 2016, and especially after 6 January 2021, journalists and scholars of Christian nationalism have focused on the charismatic Seven Mountains networks.

The critics differ among themselves. A dispensationalist and an amillennial two-kingdoms theologian agree that theonomy is wrong for opposite eschatological reasons. A secular journalist and an evangelical ethicist may both criticise Christian nationalism while disagreeing about almost everything else.
claims: Israel's civil law belonged to a unique theocratic covenant tied to the land. Christ fulfils it, and it is not a code for modern states.
Christ's kingdom advances in this age by word, Spirit and the church's witness, not by capturing political institutions.
The New Testament expects believers to live as exiles and to suffer until Christ returns. It does not promise visible cultural dominance before then.
Civil government is a common-grace institution for justice and order among believers and unbelievers alike.
Christians should take part in public life as citizens and neighbours, and should defend religious liberty for people of every faith and none.
Merging the gospel with national identity or partisan power distorts both the gospel and politics.

scriptures.reading: Christ's kingdom is not of this world. His servants do not fight to establish it, so the kingdom does not advance by political force.
Render to Caesar and to God. The two authorities are distinguished, not merged.
Believers are sojourners and exiles who honour the emperor and do good. This is the stance of a minority witness, not a governing class.
Paul quotes Deuteronomy's formula 'put away the wicked' but applies it as church discipline (excommunication), not civil execution. The Mosaic sanction is transposed for the new covenant.
The first covenant is made old and is passing away. Its theocratic structures are not simply carried forward.
Wheat and tares grow together until the harvest. The kingdom does not purge the world of unbelief before the end.
Paul tells Christians under pagan Rome to honour rulers who punish wrongdoing. Legitimate government does not need to be Christian or Mosaic.
Exiles seek the peace of the city where they live. This is a model for faithful presence rather than dominion.
The Christian's citizenship is in heaven, which relativises every earthly political identity.

arguments.text: In 1 Corinthians 5 Paul takes Deuteronomy's death-penalty formula and applies it as exclusion from the church. Critics see this as the clearest apostolic model of how Mosaic sanctions carry into the new covenant: they are transformed, not transferred to the state.
Jesus refused political kingship when offered and told Pilate his kingdom was not from this world. The apostles never asked Rome to adopt Israel's law.

Puritan Massachusetts did apply Mosaic-based laws. It banished Roger Williams (1636) and Anne Hutchinson (1638) and hanged four Quakers in Boston between 1659 and 1661. Critics cite this as evidence of what Mosaic-based civil codes do to dissenters.

American Presbyterians revised the Westminster Confession in 1788 to remove the magistrate's duty to suppress heresy. Reformed confessional history thus moved toward religious liberty, away from what theonomy would require.
Coerced faith is not faith. A gospel that calls for free response from the heart is contradicted when the state enforces religious duties, and that undermines the gospel's credibility.
'Dominion' strategies that target the top of society can reverse Jesus' pattern, in which greatness comes through service and power is shown in weakness.

critiques.from: Theonomists (Bahnsen, North)
critiques.text: Two-kingdoms and pluralist critics give public law over to secularism. There is no neutral natural law, and if not God's law then some other god's law will rule. 'Pluralism' is itself a religious claim.

critiques.from: Charismatic dominion proponents
critiques.text: Critics lump distinct people and movements under a pejorative label, rely on hostile summaries, and treat ordinary vocational and civic involvement by charismatics as sinister.

critiques.from: Conservative evangelicals wary of the 'Christian nationalism' discourse
critiques.text: Some journalistic critics use 'dominionism' and 'Christian nationalism' so broadly that any religiously motivated political activity by conservatives becomes suspect. That applies a double standard to faith-based activism on the left.

critiques.from: Postmillennialists
critiques.text: The critics' pessimism about history underrates the promises of the kingdom's growth and Christ's present reign over the nations.

responses.text: Two-kingdoms theologians answer that natural law is not neutral. It is God's law written on the heart, so Christians can argue from shared moral knowledge in public without demanding the Mosaic penal code.

Careful critics document leaders' own words and distinguish streams. Pivec and Geivett, for example, separate formal NAR leaders from charismatics generally, and Barron credits dominion teachers' concern for justice.

Several evangelical critics, such as the political scientist Paul D. Miller, distinguish Christian patriotism and civic participation from Christian nationalism. They concede that the term is sometimes overused.

Amillennial critics reply that the parables do promise real growth, but of a spiritual kingdom mixed with tares until the harvest. Christ reigns now, they say, but rules the nations through providence, not through Christian control of them.

strawMen.strawMan: Critics of dominion theology want Christians to stay out of politics.
strawMen.correction: Most critics, Reformed, dispensational and evangelical alike, encourage Christian civic participation. They object to a particular standard (the Mosaic penal code), a particular goal (Christian control of institutions) or a particular means (prophetic-political fusion).

strawMen.strawMan: Critics think God's law has nothing to say to public life.
strawMen.correction: Most affirm that the moral law, summarised in the Decalogue and known in conscience, speaks to justice in every society. Their dispute concerns the Mosaic civil code and its penalties.

strawMen.strawMan: Dominionism is a single coordinated conspiracy.
strawMen.correction: Serious critics describe overlapping networks with different theologies, not one centrally directed plot. Some popular writing has overstated the coordination, and careful critics avoid doing so.

Disagreement among critics over eschatology and natural law means they offer no single alternative vision.

Dominion means godly stewardship and influence across all seven spheres of culture.
A creation mandate given to all humanity to cultivate the earth. It is not a commission for the church to rule society, and since Genesis 9 it is exercised under common grace.
Continuity of the whole law, including civil penalties, unless the New Testament itself modifies it.
Rarely central. Most charismatic dominion teachers read it in the general evangelical sense of Christ fulfilling the law's moral intent.
'Fulfil' is christological. The law reaches its goal in Christ, and its civil form is transformed, not transferred to modern states.
Christ's kingdom does not originate from this world, but it is certainly over this world. The verse concerns the source of his authority, not its scope.
The kingdom comes by spiritual power and service rather than violence, yet it is meant to transform earthly realms.
Christ's servants do not fight for his kingdom. Its advance in this age is spiritual, not by capturing political power.
The magistrate is God's minister and must punish evil as God defines it in his law.
Government is one of the seven mountains, and godly leaders there bring justice and blessing.
Paul wrote this about pagan Rome. Legitimate government serves justice under common grace without needing to adopt Mosaic law.
God's will on earth means obedience to his law in personal, social and civil life.
A mandate to bring heaven's culture into every earthly sphere now.
A petition for the kingdom's coming that is answered partly now, in the church and in acts of mercy, and fully only at Christ's return.
Paul addresses church discipline in Corinth, where no Christian magistrate existed. The passage does not forbid civil application of Mosaic penalties where a Christian magistrate exists.
Seldom used. It is generally read as church discipline.

Christ's kingdom, set up at his first coming, steadily overcomes the kingdoms of the world in history.
The stone-become-mountain is the church rising over the mountains of culture.

Jesus affirmed the law's continuing validity down to the least commandment.
No law is neutral, so the choice is between God's law and some idol's law.
Israel's theocracy was a unique typological intrusion, not a template for common-grace states.

Paul transposes Deuteronomy's death penalty into church discipline.

Believers are called to gain godly influence at the top of the seven spheres that shape culture.

title: Word of Faith and the prosperity gospel
question: Does Scripture teach that believers can claim health and material prosperity by faith and spoken confession, and where did this teaching come from?
intro:
The Word of Faith movement, also called the faith movement or positive confession, teaches that faith is a spiritual law. Believers who believe God's promises and speak them aloud receive what they confess, and God's will for his children includes physical healing and financial prosperity. Its line of teachers runs from the evangelist E. W. Kenyon in the early twentieth century, through Kenneth Hagin, often called the movement's father, to Kenneth Copeland, Frederick K. C. Price and many televangelists. A gentler 'prosperity-lite' version, focused on positive thinking and everyday blessing, reaches huge audiences through preachers such as Joel Osteen. Historian Kate Bowler calls this 'soft prosperity'.

The movement has drawn some of the sharpest criticism in modern evangelicalism. D. R. McConnell argued that Kenyon took key ideas from New Thought metaphysics. Hank Hanegraaff called parts of the teaching heresy. Gordon Fee and the Lausanne movement challenged its exegesis and its effect on the poor. Sympathetic historians and charismatic writers, among them Joe McIntyre, Dale Simmons and William DeArteaga, have disputed the genealogy and called for reform rather than wholesale rejection.

This entry sets out three positions: the movement's own teachers, its critics, and a mediating group of revisionist historians and internal reformers.

positions.name: Word of Faith teachers
positions.summary:
Word of Faith teachers hold that God has bound himself to his word, and that faith is the means by which his promises become reality in a believer's life. Faith believes in the heart and speaks with the mouth, as in Mark 11:23 and Romans 10:10. Words carry spiritual power, so believers should confess what God's word says, not what circumstances say.

The teachers hold that Christ's redemption delivered believers from the curse of the law, which includes sickness and poverty. Healing and prosperity are therefore part of the atonement, and believers stand in Christ's authority over the devil. They see God as a good Father who wants his children well and well-supplied so that they can be generous and spread the gospel. The movement includes a 'classic' faith teaching (Kenyon, Hagin), a more explicit prosperity teaching (Copeland, Price and many others), and a softer motivational form (Osteen) that keeps the optimism and drops most of the technical doctrine.

figures.name: E. W. Kenyon
figures.profession: Evangelist, Bible school founder, radio preacher, author
figures.bio: Essek William Kenyon grew up in upstate New York. In the 1890s he spent time at the Emerson College of Oratory in Boston, a school critics link to the New Thought milieu. He founded Bethel Bible Institute in Spencer, Massachusetts (1900), and later ministered in Los Angeles and Seattle. His books on the believer's identity 'in Christ', the authority of the name of Jesus, healing and 'the two kinds of faith' became the main source on which later faith teachers drew, often closely.

works.author: E. W. Kenyon
works.title: What Happened from the Cross to the Throne

figures.name: Kenneth E. Hagin
figures.profession: Pentecostal preacher, founder of Rhema Bible Training Center
figures.bio: Hagin was a bedridden teenager in Texas with a serious heart condition. He said he was healed in 1934 after acting on Mark 11:23-24. He became an Assemblies of God pastor and then an itinerant teacher, and in 1974 founded Rhema Bible Training Center near Tulsa, which trained thousands of ministers. His plain-spoken books spread faith teaching worldwide. McConnell later showed that some passages closely reproduce Kenyon's wording. Late in life, in *The Midas Touch* (2000), Hagin criticised greed and manipulative giving appeals within the movement.

works.author: Kenneth E. Hagin
works.title: The Midas Touch: A Balanced Approach to Biblical Prosperity

figures.name: Kenneth Copeland
figures.profession: Televangelist, founder of Kenneth Copeland Ministries
figures.bio: Copeland worked as a pilot and driver for Oral Roberts and absorbed Hagin's teaching from tapes. He founded his ministry in Fort Worth, Texas, in 1967. *The Laws of Prosperity* (1974) and the *Believer's Voice of Victory* broadcasts made him the most prominent teacher of explicit prosperity doctrine. In 2007 his ministry was among six examined in a US Senate Finance Committee inquiry into the finances of religious nonprofits. The inquiry closed in 2011 with recommendations but no penalties.

figures.name: Frederick K. C. Price
figures.profession: Pastor of Crenshaw Christian Center, Los Angeles
figures.bio: Price was the most influential African American Word of Faith teacher. He was associated with Hagin from the early 1970s, built a large Los Angeles congregation, and taught healing, prosperity and positive confession on national television. He also challenged racism in the church in his later teaching.

figures.name: Joel Osteen
figures.profession: Pastor of Lakewood Church, Houston
figures.bio: Osteen succeeded his father John Osteen, a Word of Faith-influenced pastor, in 1999. He built Lakewood into one of America's largest congregations. His bestselling *Your Best Life Now* (2004) presents an upbeat message of God's favour, positive declarations and personal improvement, with little of the movement's technical doctrine. Bowler calls this 'soft prosperity'. Osteen generally avoids specific doctrinal controversy and emphasises encouragement.

positions.context:
Faith teaching grew from several nineteenth-century streams. The Holiness and Higher Life movements emphasised the believer's victory. The faith-cure movement (Charles Cullis, A. J. Gordon, A. B. Simpson, Carrie Judd Montgomery) taught healing through the atonement. New Thought and Christian Science promoted the creative power of mind. Kenyon stood where these streams met. After the Second World War, the healing revivals and Oral Roberts's 'seed-faith' teaching on giving prepared a mass audience, and Hagin's Rhema graduates and Copeland's broadcasts spread the message from the 1970s.

It has since become one of the most widespread forms of Christianity in the Global South. A 2006 Pew Forum survey of Pentecostals in ten countries found large majorities in several African, Latin American and Asian countries agreeing that God grants material prosperity to believers who have enough faith. For many poor believers the message brings dignity, hope and a reason to work and save. Critics see the same reach as a source of exploitation.
claims: Faith is believing God's word in the heart and speaking it with the mouth. Believers receive what they believe and confess according to God's promises.
Words have spiritual power, so believers should speak in agreement with Scripture rather than with symptoms or circumstances.
Christ's redemption delivered believers from the curse of the law, including sickness and poverty, so healing and prosperity belong to believers as a covenant right.
Believers share Christ's authority over Satan and may command sickness and demonic oppression to leave in Jesus' name.
God's will for his children is health and prosperity, to be used for generosity and the spread of the gospel.
Giving is sowing seed. God promises to multiply what is given in faith.
Believers are new creations who share God's nature and should understand who they are 'in Christ'.

scriptures.reading: 'Have faith in God', which Hagin rendered as 'have the God-kind of faith'. Whoever speaks to the mountain without doubting will have what he says, and what we ask in prayer we receive if we believe.
Salvation comes by believing in the heart and confessing with the mouth. This pattern of believing and confessing applies to all God's promises.
Death and life are in the power of the tongue, so negative confession invites defeat and positive confession invites blessing.
'With his stripes we are healed.' Physical healing is purchased in the atonement, as Matthew 8:17 confirms.
John wishes his readers to prosper and be in health as their soul prospers. This is God's will for every believer.
Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law. Deuteronomy 28 lists sickness and poverty among those curses, so believers are free of them.
Christ became poor so that through his poverty we might become rich. Material provision is part of the exchange at the cross.
God gives the power to get wealth in order to establish his covenant.
Those who give up things for Christ receive a hundredfold now in this time. This is the basis of the 'hundredfold return' teaching.
God calls those things which be not as though they were, and believers imitate this by speaking God's promises as already true.

arguments.text: Jesus links faith, speech and receiving in Mark 11:23-24, and the pattern recurs throughout Scripture: Abraham, the centurion, the woman with the issue of blood. Faith that speaks is a biblical category, not an invention.
Matthew applies Isaiah 53:4 to Jesus' healing ministry. So the servant's bearing of 'griefs' and 'sorrows' includes physical sickness, and healing belongs to the atonement.

The curses of Deuteronomy 28 include disease and poverty. Galatians 3:13 says Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law, and verse 14 says this was so that the blessing of Abraham, who was materially blessed, would come on the Gentiles.
If God is a good Father, he does not want his children sick and poor any more than an earthly father would. Teaching that God sends sickness to teach lessons misrepresents his character.
Prosperity is for a purpose. The gospel cannot spread without resources, and believers who are 'abounding to every good work' can fund missions and relieve the poor.

Healing through faith and the atonement was taught by respected evangelicals before the faith movement existed, among them A. B. Simpson, A. J. Gordon and Andrew Murray. Faith teachers see themselves as heirs of this tradition.
Large-scale testimonies of healing and economic uplift, especially among poor believers in Africa and Latin America, are cited as evidence that the message bears good fruit.

critiques.from: D. R. McConnell, *A Different Gospel* (1988)
critiques.text: Kenyon absorbed key ideas from New Thought and related metaphysical movements during his Boston years. These include the creative power of words, faith as a law, and a disdain for the 'sense-knowledge' of symptoms. Hagin reproduced Kenyon's material, sometimes word for word, so the movement's foundations are metaphysical rather than biblical.

critiques.from: Hank Hanegraaff, *Christianity in Crisis* (1993)
critiques.text: Some faith teachers went beyond exaggeration into serious doctrinal error: describing believers as 'little gods', teaching that Jesus died spiritually and was born again in hell, and presenting faith as a force God himself uses. These undermine the Creator-creature distinction and the sufficiency of the cross.

critiques.from: Gordon D. Fee, *The Disease of the Health and Wealth Gospels* (1985)
critiques.text: Key prooftexts are misread. 3 John 1:2 is a conventional ancient letter greeting. 'Have faith in God' in Mark 11:22 points to God as the object of faith, not to a 'God-kind' of faith-force. Jesus' and the apostles' teaching on wealth is consistently cautionary.

critiques.from: Pastoral critics and theologians of suffering
critiques.text: When healing or provision does not come, the system implies the believer's faith or confession was faulty, which adds guilt to grief. Scripture records godly people who stayed sick or poor: Paul's thorn, Trophimus left sick, Timothy's stomach, Epaphroditus near death.

critiques.from: Lausanne Theology Working Group (2008) and others concerned for the poor
critiques.text: Prosperity preaching can exploit poor people by promising returns on 'seed' gifts, while enriching leaders who live in luxury. This contradicts the apostolic warnings about greed and Jesus' teaching on the poor.

critiques.from: Kate Bowler (historian), *Blessed* (2013) and later writings
critiques.text: Bowler's historical account is descriptive and often empathetic. She documents a movement whose theology has little room for failure, chronic illness or death. After her own cancer diagnosis she wrote that the logic of 'everything happens for a reason' and deserved blessing can leave sufferers isolated.

responses.text: Defenders point out that Kenyon explicitly opposed Christian Science and claimed his teaching came from Scripture and evangelical sources. Similar themes, such as the believer's identity in Christ and faith-cure healing, appear in Higher Life writers who had nothing to do with New Thought.

Many faith teachers clarify that 'little gods' language meant sharing God's nature as his children, not becoming deity, and that they affirm the Trinity and Christ's full deity. The 'Jesus died spiritually' teaching is not held by all faith teachers and is not essential to the movement's core message.

Proponents argue that the genitive in Mark 11:22 is grammatically open. On 3 John 1:2, they say an inspired apostle would not wish for what God does not will, and the wider promises of Scripture still teach God's provision.

Hagin and others acknowledged that healing is not always instant, warned against condemning the sick, and counselled people not to abandon medical treatment. They also argue that Paul's 'thorn' was persecution, not illness.

Hagin's *The Midas Touch* (2000) itself rebuked greed, formulaic 'hundredfold' promises and manipulative fundraising. Proponents agree that abuses should be named, but argue that the teaching on God's provision stands apart from those abuses.

Supporters note that Bowler herself found genuine hope, community and economic aspiration among adherents. They reply that they do pray for and minister to the dying, and that they hold to faith while acknowledging mystery.

strawMen.strawMan: Word of Faith is just about getting rich.
strawMen.correction: The movement's core teaching concerns the believer's identity in Christ, authority, healing and the power of God's word. Prosperity is one strand, which some teachers stress far more than others.

strawMen.strawMan: Joel Osteen teaches the same doctrines as Kenneth Copeland.
strawMen.correction: Osteen's preaching is motivational 'soft prosperity'. It largely avoids the technical doctrines, such as faith as a force, spiritual death of Jesus or 'little gods', that drew the strongest criticism.

strawMen.strawMan: Faith teachers forbid doctors and medicine.
strawMen.correction: Leading teachers generally did not forbid medicine, and some explicitly warned against abandoning treatment, though individual followers have sometimes done so with tragic results.

positive: Gave many poor and marginalised believers hope, a sense of dignity and motivation toward work, saving and entrepreneurship.
Emphasised God's goodness, the believer's identity in Christ and confident prayer.
Funded and trained large numbers of ministers and missions, especially through Rhema.
Restored expectation of healing prayer in many congregations.
negative: Contributed to guilt and spiritual distress among people whose prayers for healing or provision went unanswered.
Enabled financial exploitation and extravagant lifestyles among some leaders.
Spread doctrinal statements that most Christian traditions regard as serious errors.
Tied faith to material success in ways critics see as baptising consumerism.

positions.name: Critics: evangelical, Pentecostal and historical
positions.summary:
The critics hold that the Word of Faith movement, especially its prosperity form, departs from the gospel at important points. On their reading it treats faith as a force or law rather than trust in a personal God. It turns God's promises into a formula, makes material wealth and perfect health signs of spiritual standing, and in its more extreme statements blurs the line between God and his creatures.

The critics come from different camps: cessationist and non-charismatic evangelicals, apologetics ministries, and Pentecostal scholars such as Gordon Fee who themselves believe in healing. Historians such as Kate Bowler describe rather than condemn, but their work raises related questions. Most critics affirm that God heals and provides. Their objection is to presenting these as guaranteed rights released by confession, and to the pastoral and financial damage this has done.

figures.name: D. R. McConnell

After her own stage IV cancer diagnosis, her memoir *Everything Happens for a Reason* (2018) reflected on how prosperity theology handles suffering.

figures.name: Costi W. Hinn
figures.profession: Pastor and author
figures.bio: Hinn is a nephew of the healing evangelist Benny Hinn. He grew up in and worked for his uncle's ministry before leaving it, and his book describes the prosperity world from the inside and argues for a biblical theology of money and suffering.

positions.context:
Organised criticism began in the early 1980s as faith teachers became prominent on Christian television. Apologetics ministries such as the Christian Research Institute treated the movement as a doctrinal threat. Pentecostal scholars such as Fee worried that it would discredit genuine charismatic experience. The televangelist scandals of 1987-1988, though not all involving faith teachers, sharpened public scepticism.

From the 2000s criticism became global. The Lausanne Theology Working Group met in Akropong, Ghana, in 2008 and issued a statement on the prosperity gospel, and African theologians increasingly wrote about its effects on their churches. Historians meanwhile shifted the discussion from heresy-hunting toward explaining the movement's appeal.
claims: Biblical faith is trust in a personal, sovereign God, not a spiritual force or law that obligates God when correctly applied.
The New Testament promises believers suffering, persecution and contentment in want as well as in plenty, not guaranteed wealth and health in this age.
Key prooftexts are taken out of context: 3 John 1:2, Mark 11:22-24, 2 Corinthians 8:9 and Galatians 3:13.
Some of the movement's doctrinal claims, such as 'little gods' and Jesus dying spiritually, conflict with historic Christian teaching on God and the atonement.
Prosperity preaching harms the vulnerable by blaming the sick and exploiting the poor through 'seed' appeals.
The movement's origins include significant influence from metaphysical New Thought ideas. How much influence is debated even among critics.

scriptures.reading: Godliness with contentment is great gain, and those who want to be rich fall into temptation. Paul warns against teachers who treat godliness as a means of gain (v. 5).
Paul learned contentment in abundance and in need. 'I can do all things' refers to enduring both, not to obtaining wealth.
Paul's thorn was not removed despite prayer. God's power is made perfect in weakness.
Many people of faith were tortured, destitute and afflicted, and did not receive the promise in this life. Faith does not guarantee earthly success.
A person's life does not consist in the abundance of possessions. Jesus warns against covetousness.
Our plans depend on 'if the Lord will'. Presumptuous declarations about the future are boasting.
Paul left Trophimus sick at Miletus. Even the apostle's ministry did not heal every believer.
The blind man's condition was not due to his or his parents' sin. Suffering is not always a sign of spiritual failure.
In context Christ's 'riches' given to us are spiritual. Paul uses the example to urge the Corinthians to give to the poor, not to expect material gain.

arguments.text: Read in context, 3 John 1:2 is a standard greeting formula found in ancient letters, much like 'I hope this finds you well'. It is not a doctrinal statement of God's will for universal prosperity.
Jesus and the apostles were poor by worldly standards, suffered, and promised suffering to their followers. A theology in which faith reliably produces wealth cannot account for Jesus himself.

Galatians 3:13 concerns the curse of condemnation under the law, removed so that the Gentiles receive 'the promise of the Spirit through faith' (v. 14). Paul does not say Deuteronomy's list of material curses is lifted.

McConnell documented extensive verbatim parallels between Hagin's books and Kenyon's. He also showed that Kenyon's language of 'sense-knowledge' versus 'revelation knowledge' and of faith as a law resembles New Thought writers of his Boston years.

Investigations and journalism, including a US Senate Finance Committee inquiry begun in 2007, have documented lavish lifestyles, private jets and opaque finances in several prosperity ministries. The inquiry closed in 2011 without penalties.
If faith guarantees healing, every unhealed believer must be at fault. That conclusion is pastorally destructive and contradicts biblical examples, so the premise is false.

critiques.from: Word of Faith teachers
critiques.text: Critics quote isolated statements from sermons out of context, hold the whole movement responsible for its most extreme voices, and in practice teach Christians to expect little from God.

critiques.from: Sympathetic historians (Joe McIntyre; Dale Simmons; Geir Lie)
critiques.text: The New Thought genealogy is overstated. Kenyon's main influences were Higher Life and faith-cure evangelicals, and his own writings explicitly rejected Christian Science and metaphysical religion.

critiques.from: William DeArteaga
critiques.text: Some critics bring cessationist or rationalist assumptions to the debate, so that their critique of faith teaching becomes a critique of expectant faith and the miraculous as such.

critiques.from: Scholars of global Christianity
critiques.text: Western critics sometimes ignore how prosperity teaching is actually received in poor contexts, where it can work as a theology of empowerment, discipline and hope rather than greed.

responses.text: Hanegraaff and others cite recorded broadcasts and published books at length. The updated 2009 edition of *Christianity in Crisis* added further documentation. Critics also distinguish between teachers and acknowledge that not every faith teacher holds every disputed doctrine.
Critics now often grant that Kenyon drew on both streams, as Simmons argued. They answer that the decisive question is whether the teaching agrees with Scripture, whatever its pedigree.
Several leading critics, Fee above all, were Pentecostals who believed in healing and miracles. Their critique targets a formula, not expectant faith.

Critics such as the Lausanne working group, which met in Ghana, include African voices. They acknowledge the hope and agency the message gives while arguing that it can still exploit the poor and distort the gospel.

strawMen.strawMan: Critics deny that God heals or blesses materially.
strawMen.correction: Most critics affirm that God heals and provides in answer to prayer. They deny that health and wealth are guaranteed rights claimed by confession.

strawMen.strawMan: Critics think poverty is holy and wealth sinful.
strawMen.correction: Mainstream critics hold that wealth is a stewardship with dangers, not a sin in itself, and that poverty is not a virtue but often an injustice to be relieved.

strawMen.strawMan: Every critic is a cessationist who dislikes Pentecostals.
strawMen.correction: Some of the most influential critiques came from Pentecostal and charismatic insiders: Fee, McConnell at ORU, and Hagin himself on greed.

positions.name: Revisionist historians and internal reformers
positions.summary:
A mediating group of writers, mostly charismatic, accepts that the faith movement has produced real excesses but rejects the verdict that it is a 'different gospel' at root. Joe McIntyre argued that Kenyon's sources were mainly evangelical Higher Life and faith-cure writers, not metaphysical cults. William DeArteaga argued that critics often quenched genuine spiritual insight. Dale Simmons and Geir Lie gave more mixed historical verdicts. Andrew Perriman edited a balanced report for the UK Evangelical Alliance.

Their shared position is that faith teaching recovered real biblical truths: God's goodness, the believer's authority, bold prayer and healing. These should be kept, while greed, formulaic thinking, guilt toward the sick and doctrinal overstatement are corrected. They prefer to reform the movement from within rather than reject it.

figures.profession: Pastor, president of Kenyon's Gospel Publishing Society

positions.context:
The revisionist response came in the 1990s, after McConnell and Hanegraaff had set the terms of debate. Charismatic historians felt the critiques had depended on guilt by association and had used the word 'cult' carelessly. They also observed that Hagin himself was reining in prosperity excesses by the late 1990s. His *The Midas Touch* (2000) criticised hundredfold formulas and fundraising manipulation.

The mediating position has been strongest in scholarly and denominational settings, such as the Evangelical Alliance report in the UK and Pentecostal academic discussion, and weakest in popular media, where the debate tends to polarise.
claims: Faith teaching recovered real biblical emphases: God's goodness, the believer's identity and authority in Christ, confident prayer and healing.
Kenyon's primary roots lie in evangelical Higher Life and faith-cure circles. New Thought influence was secondary at most, and how much is debated.
The movement's excesses should be corrected from within: greed, manipulative 'seed' appeals, blaming the sick, and overstatements such as 'little gods'.
Critics have often relied on guilt by association, selective quotations and cessationist or rationalist assumptions.
A balanced theology of blessing must also include suffering, contentment, generosity and God's sovereign freedom.
Historic faith teaching (Kenyon, early Hagin) should be distinguished from later fundraising-driven prosperity preaching.

scriptures.reading: Do not quench the Spirit; test everything and hold fast what is good. Test the faith movement and keep what is good.
Without faith it is impossible to please God, who rewards those who seek him. Expectant faith is commended, not suspect.
Jesus does link faith, speech and answered prayer. The fault lies in turning this into a mechanical law, not in taking it seriously.
Christians are told to think on what is true and good. Attention to the mind and thought-life is biblical even if New Thought distorted it.
God enriches believers so that they can be generous. Blessing has a purpose beyond the self.
Contentment in plenty and in want is the corrective that keeps prosperity teaching honest.
The prayer of faith shall save the sick. Healing prayer is commanded, and its exercise belongs within the church's ordinary pastoral care.

arguments.text: Kenyon's library, correspondence and sermon notes, as presented by McIntyre, show heavy dependence on A. J. Gordon, A. B. Simpson and other evangelicals, and explicit criticism of Christian Science. The genealogy of 'New Thought' is therefore at least one-sided.

Simmons and Lie, who are not partisans, both conclude that Kenyon was fundamentally an evangelical who absorbed some metaphysical vocabulary. That supports reforming the movement rather than declaring it another religion.
Scripture tells believers to test all things and hold fast to the good. Wholesale rejection of a movement through which many have come to faith and found healing ignores this instruction.
That a teaching resembles a non-Christian idea does not make it false. Early Christians used Stoic and Platonic vocabulary. The test is agreement with Scripture, not origin.
Hagin's own late correction in *The Midas Touch* shows the movement can reform itself, and that its founder did not endorse the excesses critics attribute to the whole.
Balanced biblical teaching includes both bold faith for healing and provision and contentment in suffering. The reformers seek to hold both.

critiques.from: D. R. McConnell and Hank Hanegraaff
critiques.text: Documented parallels between Kenyon's language and New Thought writers remain, even if Kenyon also read evangelicals. Calling him an evangelical does not neutralise the metaphysical elements that shaped the movement's core.

critiques.from: Evangelical and Reformed critics
critiques.text: Trimming excesses does not fix the central error. If faith is a law and confession creates reality, the system remains man-centred even when it is practised modestly.

critiques.from: Some Word of Faith teachers
critiques.text: The reformers concede too much to hostile critics and weaken bold faith by hedging every promise with caveats.

critiques.from: Historians
critiques.text: Some revisionist accounts, especially those written by people close to Kenyon's legacy, are themselves partisan and selective in their use of sources.

responses.text: Reformers reply that shared vocabulary is not shared theology. Kenyon put Christ's finished work and the authority of Scripture at the centre, which New Thought did not.
They argue that 'law of faith' language can be read as describing God's faithful pattern of response, not as an impersonal mechanism, and they urge teachers to drop language that implies the latter.
Reformers answer that biblical faith includes submission to God's will and endurance in suffering. Holding these together strengthens faith.
They welcome independent scholarship such as Simmons's and Lie's and accept its mixed verdicts as a better basis than either polemic or hagiography.

strawMen.strawMan: The reformers are simply defenders of the prosperity gospel.
strawMen.correction: They openly criticise greed, manipulation and doctrinal overstatement. Their defence is of what they see as the movement's biblical core, not of its abuses.

strawMen.strawMan: Revisionists claim Kenyon had no contact at all with New Thought.
strawMen.correction: McIntyre minimises the influence, but Simmons and Lie accept some influence and argue only that it was secondary to evangelical sources.

positive: Raised the standard of historical research on the movement's origins.
Offered a path for charismatic churches to keep bold faith while rejecting abuses.
Modelled more charitable debate between critics and adherents.
negative: Can give cover to teachers who use 'balance' language while continuing questionable practices.
Has had limited influence on the popular, broadcast face of the movement.

readings.reading: 'Have the God-kind of faith.' Believe in the heart, speak to the mountain, and you will have what you say.
'Have faith in God.' God is the object of faith. The saying is a vivid encouragement to trust, set in the context of judgment on the fruitless temple, not a law of speech.
A genuine promise linking faith and prayer, which should be taken boldly, but always within God's will and not as a mechanism.
God's will is that believers prosper and be in health as their souls prosper.
A conventional letter greeting wishing Gaius well. It is not a doctrinal promise.
It shows that well-being is a fitting Christian wish and prayer, though not a guaranteed right.
Physical healing is purchased in the atonement and available to faith now.
Primarily about healing from sin. The atonement secures bodily healing finally at the resurrection, and Matthew 8:17 shows it beginning in Jesus' ministry without guaranteeing it now.
The atonement is the ground of all healing, so believers may pray boldly, but the timing belongs to God.
Christ became poor so that we could become materially rich.
The riches are spiritual, and Paul uses Christ's example to urge generosity to the poor in Jerusalem.
Primarily spiritual riches, though God does supply believers so that they can be generous (2 Cor 9:8-11).
Redemption from the curse covers every curse of Deuteronomy 28, including sickness and poverty.
Redemption from the law's condemnation, so that Gentiles receive the Spirit by faith. Material curses are not the subject.
Centrally about justification and the Spirit, but the blessing of Abraham has whole-life implications that faith may lay hold of.
Paul's thorn was a messenger of Satan, meaning persecution, not sickness. Grace was sufficient to endure opposition.
Whatever the thorn was, God refused to remove it. Power is perfected in weakness, which refutes guaranteed deliverance.
A reminder that some prayers are answered with grace to endure rather than removal. Faith teaching must include this.
Words carry creative spiritual power for life or death, so confess God's word.
A wisdom saying about the consequences of speech in human relationships. It is not about words creating reality.
Speech shapes our lives and communities, so speak faith and truth, without claiming that words compel God.

title: The modern prophetic movement and the New Apostolic Reformation
question: Has God restored the offices of apostle and prophet to the church today, and how should claims of prophetic revelation be tested?
intro:
Since the 1980s a large network of charismatic leaders has taught that God is restoring the 'fivefold' ministries of Ephesians 4:11, especially prophets and apostles, as active offices that govern and guide the church. Leaders in this movement claim prophetic revelation for individuals, churches and nations, and organise their churches into apostolic networks rather than denominations. C. Peter Wagner named the apostolic side of this development the 'New Apostolic Reformation' (NAR). Its prophetic side includes the 'Kansas City Prophets', Bill Hamon's Christian International and Cindy Jacobs's Generals International.

Critics, including cessationists and continuationists such as Holly Pivec and R. Douglas Geivett, argue that the movement misreads the New Testament on apostles, sets aside the biblical tests for prophecy, and concentrates unaccountable authority in a few leaders. A third group of charismatics and Pentecostals believes prophecy continues today but has pressed for internal reform, especially after many prophetic words about the 2020 US election failed. Their efforts include Michael Brown's advocacy and the Prophetic Standards statement.

All three groups appeal to the biblical tests for prophecy: Deuteronomy 18:20-22, 1 Thessalonians 5:20-21, 1 Corinthians 14:29 and 1 John 4:1. They disagree about how those tests apply under the new covenant.

positions.name: Apostolic-prophetic movement (NAR and allied prophets)
positions.summary:
Proponents believe that God has progressively restored truths and ministries to the church since the Reformation. On Bill Hamon's account this ran from justification by faith, through holiness and Pentecostal power, to a restored prophetic ministry in the 1980s and a restored apostolic ministry in the 1990s.

On this view Ephesians 4:11-13 lists five gifts Christ gave 'till we all come' to maturity, so apostles and prophets did not end with the first century. Present-day apostles give governmental oversight to networks of churches. Prophets receive revelation for individuals, congregations and nations, including direction for spiritual warfare and for cultural transformation. Most proponents distinguish New Testament prophecy from Scripture: it adds nothing to the canon, is partial ('we prophesy in part') and must be judged. A prophet can therefore be mistaken without being a false prophet in the sense of Deuteronomy 18. Many leaders who share these practices reject the 'NAR' label and say there is no single organised movement.

figures.name: C. Peter Wagner
figures.profession: Missiologist, Fuller Theological Seminary professor, apostolic network convener
figures.bio: Wagner served as a missionary in Bolivia and then taught church growth at Fuller Seminary's School of World Mission for three decades. In the 1990s he described a fast-growing 'post-denominational' church led by apostles and named it the New Apostolic Reformation. He convened the International Coalition of Apostles (1999) and the Apostolic Council of Prophetic Elders, and founded Wagner Leadership Institute. He also championed strategic-level spiritual warfare. In 2008 he publicly expressed regret for having taken part in the apostolic commissioning of Todd Bentley during the Lakeland revival.

figures.name: Bill Hamon
figures.profession: Bishop, founder of Christian International Ministries Network
figures.bio: Hamon founded Christian International in 1967; it is now based in Santa Rosa Beach, Florida. He has trained thousands in 'prophetic ministry' and personal prophecy. His books set out a restoration history in which a 'prophetic movement' was birthed in the late 1980s and an 'apostolic movement' in the late 1990s, and they give guidelines for receiving, recording and judging personal prophecy.

figures.profession: Co-founder of Generals International, prophetic teacher
figures.bio: Jacobs co-founded Generals of Intercession, later Generals International, in 1985. She became one of the movement's best-known prophetic voices. Her books on intercession and on hearing God popularised prophetic prayer and 'reformation' of nations, and she was a central figure in Wagner's Apostolic Council of Prophetic Elders.

figures.name: Paul Cain
figures.profession: Healing evangelist and prophet
figures.bio: Cain ministered in the post-war healing revivals of the 1950s, including alongside William Branham, then largely withdrew from public ministry. He re-emerged in the late 1980s as the most celebrated of the 'Kansas City Prophets' and was known for detailed predictive words. In 2004 Mike Bickle, Jack Deere and Rick Joyner publicly stated that Cain had struggled with homosexual behaviour and alcoholism and was being restored. The disclosure deepened critics' concerns about character and accountability.
