figures.name: Mike Bickle
figures.profession: Founder of Kansas City Fellowship and the International House of Prayer Kansas City (IHOPKC)
figures.bio: Bickle led the Kansas City Fellowship from the early 1980s, the church that hosted the Kansas City Prophets. It joined John Wimber's Vineyard in 1990 amid controversy. In 1999 he founded IHOPKC, a round-the-clock prayer ministry with a strong end-times emphasis and international influence. In late 2023 IHOPKC ended its relationship with him following allegations of past sexual misconduct.

positions.context:
The movement draws on the 1948 Latter Rain revival in Saskatchewan, which taught restored apostles and prophets, laying on of hands to impart gifts, and an end-time 'manifested' church. The Assemblies of God rejected it in 1949. The ideas survived in independent networks and resurfaced through the 1970s charismatic renewal. In the late 1980s John Wimber's Vineyard briefly brought the Kansas City Prophets to a wide evangelical audience. In the 1990s Wagner's research on fast-growing independent churches in the Global South and the United States gave the apostolic side a name and an organisational form.

The movement is global and decentralised. Wagner estimated hundreds of millions of adherents worldwide, a figure critics and scholars treat with caution. Prophetic conferences, schools of ministry and media platforms spread its practices well beyond formal networks. After 2016, high-profile prophecies about American politics brought it unusual public attention.
claims: Christ gave apostles, prophets, evangelists, pastors and teachers 'till we all come' to maturity, so all five remain until the church is complete.
God has restored the offices of prophet (from the 1980s) and apostle (from the 1990s) as part of a progressive restoration of the church.
Apostles exercise governmental authority over networks of churches and ministries, and prophets give revelation to guide them.
Prophets receive revelation for individuals, churches, cities and nations, including predictive words.
New Testament prophecy does not add to Scripture, is partial, and must be weighed. Inaccurate words call for correction, not automatic condemnation as a false prophet.
Strategic-level spiritual warfare against territorial spirits is part of advancing God's kingdom.
The restored apostolic and prophetic ministries prepare the church for end-time harvest and for transforming society.

scriptures.reading: The five gifts are given 'till we all come' to the unity of the faith and a perfect man. Since that goal has not been reached, apostles and prophets continue.
The church is built on the foundation of apostles and prophets. Every generation needs foundation-laying ministry for new churches and nations.
God has set in the church first apostles, secondly prophets. The order describes the church's permanent structure, not a first-century exception.
Prophets and teachers at Antioch heard the Spirit commission Barnabas and Saul. This is a model for prophetic direction of mission.
Agabus predicted a famine, and the church acted on it. Predictive prophecy guides practical decisions.
God does nothing without revealing his secret to his servants the prophets. Prophets are needed to discern what God is doing.
God promised to pour out his Spirit on all flesh so that sons and daughters prophesy, a promise for the whole church age (Acts 2:17-18).
We prophesy in part. New Testament prophecy is real but partial, which explains why prophets can be wrong in details.
Believers wrestle against principalities and powers, which supports strategic warfare against spiritual powers over regions.

arguments.text: Ephesians 4:11-13 ties all five ministries to the same purpose and the same time span, 'till we all come' to maturity. Removing the first two while keeping the other three is arbitrary.

The New Testament names apostles beyond the Twelve and Paul, such as Barnabas, James the Lord's brother, Andronicus and Junia, and possibly Silas and Timothy. So 'apostle' is not limited to eyewitnesses of the resurrection.
Paul commands believers to desire to prophesy and not to forbid it, and to judge prophecies rather than reject them. That presumes ongoing, fallible congregational prophecy.

Prophecy and visions continued after the apostles, in the *Didache*'s instructions on testing travelling prophets, in second-century accounts and in later revival movements. On this view cessation was a later theological assumption, not the church's original experience.
Rapid church growth in independent apostolic networks in Africa, Latin America and Asia, which Wagner documented as a missiologist, is presented as fruit validating the model.
Denominational bureaucracy tends to slow mission. Relational apostolic networks allow quicker, Spirit-led response, as in the book of Acts.

critiques.from: Holly Pivec and R. Douglas Geivett
critiques.text: The movement claims for its apostles and prophets a governmental authority and revelatory role that the New Testament gives only to the foundational apostles and prophets. In practice this places followers under leaders whose words function like extra-biblical revelation.

critiques.from: Cessationist critics (e.g. John MacArthur)
critiques.text: Deuteronomy 18 requires that a prophet who speaks presumptuously in God's name must not be heeded. The movement's record of failed predictions, especially about the 2020 US election, exposes the gift as counterfeit.

critiques.from: Ernie Gruen and other charismatic critics (1990)
critiques.text: Gruen, a Kansas City pastor, documented what he saw as manipulative prophecy, elitism and doctrinal error at Kansas City Fellowship. Later moral failures involving leading prophets confirmed fears about character and accountability.

critiques.from: Assemblies of God position paper 'Apostles and Prophets' (2001)
critiques.text: Classical Pentecostals welcomed apostolic and prophetic ministry functions but warned against self-appointed offices claiming authority over churches and against restoring Latter Rain errors that the denomination had rejected in 1949.

critiques.from: Journalists and scholars of religion and politics
critiques.text: Politicised prophecy, such as declaring election outcomes and casting political opponents as demonic, has damaged the credibility of the prophetic gift and contributed to unrest after the 2020 election.

responses.text: Wagner and others answered that today's apostles do not write Scripture and are not equal to the Twelve. Their authority is relational and functional, and it is accepted voluntarily by those who align with them.

Proponents argue that Deuteronomy 18 governed Old Testament canonical prophets. New Testament prophecy is 'in part' and is to be weighed, so a mistaken word calls for correction and repentance, not stoning or automatic dismissal.

Leaders including John Wimber and Mike Bickle acknowledged errors in the early Kansas City period and introduced correction. Defenders argue that the sins of individuals do not invalidate a biblical gift.
Many apostolic leaders agree with warnings against self-appointment and point to their own accountability structures, such as apostolic councils, alignment and mutual submission.

Some prophets apologised publicly for 2020 election words, and many leaders now caution against partisan prophecy. Defenders add that political prophecies are a small fraction of prophetic ministry, most of which concerns individuals and local churches.

strawMen.strawMan: NAR prophets claim their words are equal to Scripture.
strawMen.correction: Most proponents explicitly say prophecy today is subordinate to Scripture and must be tested by it. Critics' concern is that in practice prophetic words can function with near-scriptural authority.

strawMen.strawMan: The NAR is a single organisation with a membership list.
strawMen.correction: It is a loose web of networks, ministries and teachings. Many leaders who share its practices reject the label, which is why both proponents and careful critics describe it as a movement, not a denomination.

strawMen.strawMan: Everyone who believes in prophecy today belongs to the NAR.
strawMen.correction: Most continuationists, including many Pentecostal denominations, practise prophecy without accepting apostolic offices with governmental authority. Some are strong critics of the NAR.

positive: Renewed expectancy for the Spirit's gifts and for hearing God among many believers.
Fuelled extensive prayer movements, such as 24-hour prayer rooms, and missionary energy.
Supported fast-growing independent churches in the Global South with flexible leadership structures.
negative: Failed predictions, especially in 2020, damaged public trust in prophecy.
Leader-centred networks with weak accountability have been linked to several moral and spiritual-abuse scandals.
Fusion of prophecy with partisan politics divided churches.
Some followers have made life decisions on prophetic words that later proved mistaken.

positions.name: Critics of the apostolic-prophetic movement
positions.summary:
Critics argue that the movement misreads the New Testament on apostles and prophets, and so creates a class of leaders who claim revelatory authority that Scripture does not give. They come from two camps.

Cessationists such as John MacArthur hold that revelatory gifts ended with the apostolic age and the closing of the canon. Continuationist and non-committal evangelicals such as Holly Pivec and R. Douglas Geivett, who deliberately do not rest their case on cessationism, argue that even if spiritual gifts continue, the NAR's particular claims are unbiblical: governing apostles, prophets who direct nations, strategic-level spiritual warfare and new revelation for the church's mission.

Both camps stress the biblical tests of prophecy, the sufficiency of Scripture, the accountability of leaders, and the documented record of failed predictions and moral scandals.

figures.bio: MacArthur is the best-known contemporary cessationist critic of the charismatic movement. His broad brush drew criticism from continuationist evangelicals.

figures.profession: New Testament scholar, Southern Baptist Theological Seminary

He made the case with notable charity toward continuationists.

positions.context:
Criticism started inside the charismatic world, with Gruen's 1990 report on Kansas City and with classical Pentecostal concern about the revival of Latter Rain ideas, which led to the Assemblies of God's 2001 paper on apostles and prophets. Wagner's use of the 'NAR' label made the movement easier to analyse. In 2011 a radio interview and press coverage linking the NAR to political 'dominionism' prompted Wagner to publish a response defending the movement and denying theocratic aims.

After 2016, and especially after the failed 2020 election prophecies and 6 January 2021, criticism from evangelicals, ex-members and journalists grew sharply. Former participants added testimony about spiritual abuse.
claims: The apostles of Ephesians 2:20 were a unique foundational group, eyewitnesses commissioned by the risen Christ, and that foundation has been laid once for all.
Scripture is sufficient and the faith has been once delivered. No present-day leader can claim revelatory authority to direct the church.
Biblical tests of prophecy include accuracy (Deuteronomy 18), orthodoxy (Deuteronomy 13; 1 John 4) and character (Matthew 7). Many modern prophets fail them.
Governing apostolic offices outside accountable church structures foster authoritarianism and spiritual abuse.
Practices such as strategic-level spiritual warfare and spiritual mapping lack biblical warrant.
Political prophecy has harmed the church's witness and treated partisan causes as the will of God.

scriptures.reading: A prophet whose prediction in the Lord's name does not come to pass has spoken presumptuously and is not to be feared.
Even a prophet whose sign comes true is false if he leads people after other gods. Accuracy alone is not enough.
The apostles and prophets are the foundation, with Christ the cornerstone. A foundation is laid once and then built upon.
An apostle in the full sense had to be a witness of Jesus' ministry and resurrection.
Paul calls himself the last to whom the risen Christ appeared, 'as of one born out of due time'. The line of resurrection witnesses closes with him.
God has spoken finally in his Son in these last days. The era of new revelation culminates in Christ and the apostolic witness.
The faith was once for all delivered to the saints, not progressively revealed through new prophets.
False prophets are known by their fruits. Character and outcomes matter.
Prophets who speak a vision of their own heart, not from the Lord's mouth, are not to be heeded.
Paul warns of 'false apostles' and 'super-apostles' who transform themselves into apostles of Christ.

arguments.text: Ephesians 2:20 makes apostles and prophets the church's foundation. Ephesians 3:5 says the mystery was revealed to them. Their role was to lay down revelation, so it is unrepeatable, just as a building gets one foundation.

Apostleship in the governing sense required having seen the risen Lord and being personally commissioned, and Paul presents himself as the last such witness. The wider 'apostles' (Barnabas and others) were missionary envoys of churches, not governing officers over networks.
Deuteronomy 18 gives a clear accuracy test that the New Testament never revokes. Prophecies about specific outcomes, such as elections, pandemics and dates, that do not happen fall under it.

The movement's own history includes repeated failed predictions and moral collapses among celebrated prophets. Examples include the Kansas City controversies of 1990, the Lakeland revival of 2008 and its aftermath, and many 2020 election prophecies. Critics read this as a pattern, not as isolated lapses.

The Assemblies of God rejected the 1948 Latter Rain movement's restoration of apostles and prophets in 1949, and reaffirmed caution in 2001. Classical Pentecostals have therefore long seen the NAR's distinctive claims as an aberration.

If apostles have governing authority and prophets speak for God, followers have no practical way to dissent without seeming to resist God. That structure invites abuse regardless of any leader's intentions.

critiques.from: Apostolic-prophetic leaders
critiques.text: Critics create a monolithic 'NAR' that does not exist, attribute fringe statements to everyone, and quote selectively from leaders who reject the label.

critiques.from: Continuationist scholars (e.g. Wayne Grudem, Sam Storms)
critiques.text: Applying Deuteronomy 18's death-penalty standard to New Testament congregational prophecy ignores Paul's instruction to weigh prophecies, which presupposes that some will be partly wrong.

critiques.from: Continuationist critics of cessationism (e.g. Michael Brown, *Authentic Fire*)
critiques.text: Cessationist critics like MacArthur condemn the whole charismatic movement, hundreds of millions of believers, on the basis of its worst examples. That is unfair and unbiblical.

critiques.from: Global South church leaders
critiques.text: Western critics may misread apostolic leadership in contexts where informal, charismatic leadership is the normal and effective form of church growth.

responses.text: Pivec and Geivett distinguish a 'formal' NAR, meaning leaders who adopt the offices and teachings explicitly, from a wider 'informal' influence, and they document views from leaders' own writings. Wagner himself coined and used the label.

Critics such as Schreiner argue that Agabus's prophecy in Acts 21 was substantially accurate. On this reading 'weighing' prophecy means judging whether it is from God, not sorting true parts from false parts of a genuine prophecy.

Non-cessationist critics such as Pivec and Geivett explicitly avoid blanket condemnation and focus on specific teachings. Even some cessationists acknowledge that individual charismatics may be sincere believers.

Critics respond that the issue is not leadership style but claims of revelatory authority. They note that African and Latin American theologians have themselves criticised abuses by self-styled apostles and prophets.

strawMen.strawMan: Critics of the NAR are all cessationists who deny the Spirit's gifts.
strawMen.correction: Several prominent critics, including classical Pentecostals and continuationist evangelicals, affirm present-day gifts and object specifically to governing apostles and directive prophets.

strawMen.strawMan: Critics think every prophetic word is demonic.
strawMen.correction: Most critics attribute failed prophecies to human imagination, presumption or misunderstanding, as in Jeremiah 23:16, rather than to demonic deception. Some cessationists do warn of spiritual deception.

positive: Gave pastors and families vocabulary and resources to evaluate teachings entering their churches.
Pressed for accountability and documented patterns of failed prophecy and abuse.
Contributed to internal reforms within the charismatic world.
negative: Broad cessationist polemic has alienated many sincere charismatics and hardened divisions.
The 'NAR' label is sometimes applied loosely to any charismatic church.
Debates have sometimes become personal rather than exegetical.

adherents: Cessationist Reformed and Baptist evangelicals
Many classical Pentecostal leaders cautious of Latter Rain ideas
Continuationist evangelicals critical of NAR distinctives
Former participants in apostolic-prophetic networks

positions.name: Continuationist reformers: prophecy with accountability
positions.summary:
A third group believes that prophecy and other spiritual gifts continue today, but insists that they be practised under clear biblical guardrails. Following Wayne Grudem's influential argument, it treats ordinary New Testament prophecy as a human report of something God brings to mind. Such prophecy is fallible and lacks the authority of Scripture, and it must be weighed by the church.

The reformers often favour a 'functional' view of apostles, meaning pioneering church planters and missionaries, over a governing office equal to the Twelve. They call prophets to public accountability for failed words, warn against partisan and date-setting prophecy, and insist that character counts for more than gifting. After the failed 2020 election prophecies, voices such as Michael Brown called for repentance and helped promote the Prophetic Standards statement. Earlier, J. Lee Grady and Sam Storms had written practical correctives.

figures.name: Wayne Grudem
figures.profession: Systematic theologian, Phoenix Seminary
figures.bio: Grudem is a Reformed Baptist continuationist. His 1988 book argued that New Testament congregational prophecy differs from Old Testament and apostolic revelation: it is fallible and must be evaluated, and it does not threaten the sufficiency of Scripture. This 'two-tier' view gave many evangelicals a framework for openness to prophecy with guardrails.

figures.profession: Messianic Jewish apologist, radio host, scholar of Semitic languages
figures.bio: Brown is a charismatic who has defended continuationism against MacArthur and also criticised excesses within his own movement. After the failed 2020 election prophecies he called repeatedly for prophets to acknowledge error publicly. He was a leading promoter of the Prophetic Standards statement, which set out ethical and accountability guidelines for prophetic ministry.

figures.bio: Storms was once a cessationist. After time with John Wimber's Vineyard and the Kansas City prophetic community he became a Reformed charismatic. His books give careful, practical guidance on practising prophecy humbly and testing it by Scripture.

figures.profession: Journalist, former editor of *Charisma* magazine
figures.bio: As editor of the leading charismatic magazine, Grady regularly criticised abuses inside the movement. His targets included unaccountable 'apostles', prophetic manipulation, and the 2008 Lakeland revival and its fallout.

works.title: The Holy Spirit Is Not for Sale

figures.name: John Wimber
figures.profession: Founding leader of the Association of Vineyard Churches
figures.bio: Wimber brought the Kansas City Prophets into the Vineyard in 1990 and tried to correct their practice with stronger pastoral oversight and biblical teaching. Later in the 1990s he distanced the Vineyard from some prophetic emphases. His approach, openness with accountability, became a model for later reformers.

positions.context:
Reform efforts have come in waves after crises. Wimber's oversight of the Kansas City Prophets followed the 1990 Gruen controversy. Critiques followed the Lakeland revival in 2008. The largest wave followed 2020, when numerous well-known prophets had confidently predicted Donald Trump's re-election. Some, such as Jeremiah Johnson in January 2021, publicly apologised and reported receiving harsh backlash from followers. Others reinterpreted their words or kept to them.

The Prophetic Standards statement followed in 2021. It was drafted by charismatic leaders and called for accountability, humility, correction of failed words and avoidance of manipulation. Supporters see it as a sign the movement can police itself. Sceptics note that it has no enforcement mechanism.
claims: Prophecy continues as a gift for the church's edification, exhortation and comfort, and believers should earnestly desire it.
Ordinary New Testament prophecy is fallible human speech prompted by revelation. It never equals Scripture and must be weighed.
'Apostle' today is best understood functionally (church planter, missionary, pioneer), not as a governing office equal to the Twelve.
Prophets must publicly acknowledge and correct failed words, and churches should hold them accountable.
Prophetic ministry should avoid partisan politics, date-setting, control and financial manipulation.
Character, fruit and orthodoxy are essential tests alongside accuracy.

scriptures.reading: Prophecy speaks to people for edification, exhortation and comfort. Its normal purpose is upbuilding, not direction of nations.
Let two or three prophets speak and the others weigh what is said. Prophecy is subject to communal evaluation.
Do not despise prophecies, but test everything. This rules out both blanket rejection and naive acceptance.
Test the spirits, because many false prophets have gone out. Testing is a standing duty.
Presumptuous prediction is serious. Even if New Testament prophecy is not under the death penalty, prophets who miss must own it and not be trusted blindly.
Agabus's prophecy was broadly true but arguably inexact in detail (compare 21:33). Grudem uses it as an example of fallible New Testament prophecy.
Prophetic power without love is nothing. Character matters more than gift.
Some who prophesied in Jesus' name will be disowned. Gifting is no proof of approval.

arguments.text: Paul treats prophecy as something to be weighed and partly sifted. That implies congregational prophecy could include error without the speaker being a false prophet, which distinguishes it from canonical prophecy.
Paul tells the church to desire prophecy and not to forbid tongues, so wholesale cessation contradicts apostolic instruction. Paul is equally clear that 'all things be done decently and in order'.

The *Didache* (late first or early second century) both welcomed travelling prophets and gave practical tests: a prophet who asked for money or overstayed was false. Reformers see this as the earliest model of accountable prophecy.
Failed prophecies in 2020 and the subsequent apologies show the need for formal standards. Without accountability, the gift's credibility collapses.
Treating prophecy as fallible protects the sufficiency of Scripture and lets the church practise the gift without making every word binding.

critiques.from: Cessationist scholars (e.g. Richard Gaffin, Thomas Schreiner)
critiques.text: 'Fallible prophecy' is a category the Bible does not know. In Scripture, prophecy is God's word; if a word can be wrong, it is not prophecy. Agabus's prophecy was not erroneous.

critiques.from: Apostolic-prophetic leaders
critiques.text: Reformers can quench the Spirit and create a culture of fear around prophetic ministry. Public 'calling out' of prophets violates honour and should be handled privately.

critiques.from: Critics such as Pivec and Geivett
critiques.text: Standards statements lack enforcement. Many prophets whose 2020 words failed continued their ministries with large followings and without public retraction.

critiques.from: Historians of the movement
critiques.text: Similar reform moments in 1990 and 2008 did not prevent later crises. Without structural change, reform statements may be cyclical damage control.

responses.text: Grudem and others reply that Paul's instruction to weigh prophecies and not 'despise' them would make no sense if every genuine prophecy were infallible. They also argue that the Greek usage of 'prophet' in the New Testament era was broader than canonical prophecy.
Reformers answer that the same verse that says 'quench not the Spirit' goes on to say 'prove all things'. Public prophecies, especially about nations, require public correction.

Reformers acknowledge the enforcement gap. They argue that the remedy lies in local church accountability and in congregants choosing whom to follow, not in a central authority, which their ecclesiology lacks.
They accept the historical point and argue that each crisis has nonetheless produced growing consensus around Scripture's primacy, prophetic humility and pastoral oversight.

strawMen.strawMan: Reformers are cessationists in disguise.
strawMen.correction: They practise and encourage prophecy and other gifts. Their concern is how prophecy is practised, not whether it exists.

strawMen.strawMan: Fallible prophecy means prophets can say anything without consequence.
strawMen.correction: Reformers argue the opposite. Because prophecy is fallible it must be tested, and repeated failure should disqualify someone from public prophetic ministry.

positive: Gave continuationist churches a framework to practise prophecy without undermining Scripture.
Produced public apologies and clearer ethical standards after 2020.
Modelled self-critique within the charismatic movement.
negative: Reform statements have had limited reach among high-profile independent prophets.
The 'fallible prophecy' concept is contested and, critics say, may lower the stakes of speaking in God's name.

adherents: Reformed charismatics and many Vineyard churches
Pentecostal and charismatic scholars and pastors seeking accountability
Evangelical continuationists influenced by Grudem
Signatories and supporters of the Prophetic Standards statement

readings.reading: All five gifts, including apostles and prophets, last 'till we all come' to maturity, so the offices continue today.
The gifts serve maturity, but Ephesians 2:20 shows the apostles and prophets as the once-laid foundation. Their continuing function is through their recorded teaching.
The functions continue: pioneering apostolic work and prophetic encouragement. A governing office equal to the Twelve does not.
Every new church and nation needs foundation-laying apostolic and prophetic ministry.
A foundation is laid once. The apostles and prophets of the first century gave the church its revealed basis.
The foundational apostles and prophets are unique. Present prophecy builds on that foundation and never adds to it.
This applied to Old Testament covenant prophets. New Testament prophecy is 'in part', and mistakes call for correction.
A permanent test. Prophets whose specific predictions fail have spoken presumptuously and should not be heeded.
The death penalty does not carry over, but the principle does: failed predictions must be owned, and repeated failure disqualifies.
Prophecy is weighed, normally by other mature prophets and leaders.
The church judges whether a message is from God at all. Weighing does not mean accepting a mixture of truth and error as genuine prophecy.
The whole congregation weighs prophecy, which shows it is fallible and subordinate to Scripture.
Do not despise prophecy. Critics who reject it wholesale disobey this command.
'Prove all things.' Testing is mandatory, and much modern prophecy fails the test.
Both halves matter: neither despise nor accept uncritically.
Agabus models New Testament predictive prophecy that guides the church.
Agabus's prophecy was accurate in substance. It is an example of reliable prophecy, not fallible prophecy.
On Grudem's reading, Agabus was right in substance but inexact in detail (the Romans, not the Jews, bound Paul), which shows New Testament prophecy is fallible.
God's final word is Christ. Present prophecy points to him and adds no new doctrine.
With the Son's coming, revelation reaches its climax. Claims to ongoing directive revelation undermine this finality.
Christ is God's final word. Prophecy today applies, never adds to, that revelation.

timeline.title: Latter Rain revival
timeline.note: At North Battleford, Saskatchewan, a revival teaches restored apostles and prophets and impartation by laying on of hands.

timeline.title: Assemblies of God rejects Latter Rain
timeline.note: The General Council adopts a resolution disapproving of the 'New Order of the Latter Rain'.

timeline.title: Kansas City Fellowship
timeline.note: Mike Bickle's church becomes the home of the 'Kansas City Prophets'.

timeline.title: Prophetic movement and Grudem
timeline.note: Bill Hamon dates the restoration of the prophetic movement to this period, and Wayne Grudem publishes his fallible-prophecy thesis.

timeline.title: Gruen report and Vineyard
timeline.note: Ernie Gruen circulates his critique of Kansas City Fellowship, and John Wimber brings the church into the Vineyard to provide oversight.

timeline.title: Naming the movement
timeline.note: Around this time C. Peter Wagner begins promoting the term 'New Apostolic Reformation', including through a Fuller Seminary symposium on post-denominational churches.

timeline.title: International Coalition of Apostles
timeline.note: Wagner convenes a coalition of self-identified apostles, and the Apostolic Council of Prophetic Elders begins issuing words.

timeline.title: AG paper on apostles and prophets
timeline.note: The Assemblies of God adopts a position paper affirming apostolic and prophetic functions but rejecting self-appointed governing offices.

timeline.title: Paul Cain disclosure
timeline.note: Bickle, Jack Deere and Rick Joyner publicly disclose Cain's moral failures.

timeline.title: Lakeland revival
timeline.note: Wagner and others commission Todd Bentley. Bentley's marital collapse follows soon after, and Wagner publicly expresses regret.

timeline.title: Public scrutiny and Wagner's reply
timeline.note: Media coverage links the NAR to political dominionism, and Wagner publishes a response denying theocratic aims.

timeline.title: Pivec and Geivett
timeline.note: *A New Apostolic Reformation?* offers a detailed evangelical critique.

timeline.title: Failed election prophecies
timeline.note: Numerous prophets predict Donald Trump's re-election. The failure prompts apologies, reinterpretations and controversy.

timeline.title: Apologies and Prophetic Standards
timeline.note: Jeremiah Johnson publicly apologises in January. Charismatic leaders, Michael Brown prominent among them, promote a Prophetic Standards statement on accountability. The exact date and signatories need checking.

timeline.title: IHOPKC crisis
timeline.note: IHOPKC separates from founder Mike Bickle after allegations of past sexual misconduct, renewing debate about accountability.

Weighing prophecies would be pointless if all genuine prophecy were infallible.
